Fine motor:
A short hands-on screen looked at how xx manages the fine motor tasks of the school day.

* Pencil grasp and bilateral coordination– She uses a dynamic tripod grasp when writing. She rested her helper hand in her lap at first, but held the paper steady after a verbal cue..
* Coloring – She colored a 2-inch star and stayed within the border on all but one point.
* Cutting – During cutting tasks, she opened and closed the scissors with a smooth rhythm and turned the paper with her helper hand. She cut a complex shape (heart) with two small deviations.
* Tool Use – She managed classroom tools such as a glue stick and tape without help.
* Handwriting Sample – When given a two-sentence (14 words) sample to copy, she spaced her words evenly, used lowercase letters where expected, and kept letters on the baseline for 80% of words. However, her letters drifted larger toward the end of each line, she skipped the word "to," and she misspelled one word ("jmup" for "jump"). However, her overall writing is within normal age expectations. Her classroom writing sample showed the same drift in size and a tendency to crowd the right margin. When asked to recall the alphabet from memory without cues, she recalled 24/26 uppercase and lowercase letters, demonstrating reversals on J and S. When provided with cues during letter copying, she demonstrated the motor skills to copy all uppercase and lowercase letters without letter reversals or incorrect formation, suggesting functional motor skills. Overall, her writing was generally legible, though primarily impacted by letter size, suggesting she may benefit from paper with a highlighted writing zone, as well as a visual reminder to leave a margin.

Sensory Processing:
Sensory processing is how a person takes in sights, sounds, touch and movement and makes use of them.  Differences in sensory processing can change how a student attends, moves and joins in at school.
During clinical observations, XX demonstrated difficulty with sustained attention, often leaving his chair to look out of the window and humming while he worked, which impacted his ability to sustain attention during testing.
The SPM-2 school questionnaire was filled in by XX’s teacher to show which kinds of sensory input get in the way of his day in class.  It covers these areas:  Social Participation, Vision, Hearing, Touch, Taste and Smell, Body Awareness, Balance and Motion, Planning and Ideas.  Each area is reported as Typical, Moderate Difficulties, or Severe Difficulties.  XX results are listed here:
Typical Processing:

* Taste and Smell
* Vision

Moderate Difficulties:

* Social Participation
* Touch

Severe Difficulties:

* Hearing
* Body awareness
* Balance and Motion
* Planning and ideas
* Sensory total

Teacher checklist
On a classroom checklist, the special education teacher marked fine motor tasks as hard for XX on most school days, which gets in the way of his independence in class. The tasks marked were letter sizing, line adherence, coloring, cutting, buttoning, and opening containers.  Legibility, letter formation, staying on the line, and spacing were also marked.  The teacher also noted sensory behaviors, a habit of chewing on his sleeves and covering his ears during assemblies, that pull him away from lessons. Supports already used in class are a chewable pencil topper, a seat near the door, and a visual schedule.

Impact Statement

XX [XX disability]] affects his hand skills, self-care, and sensory processing at school. Because writing is hard, he cannot always show what he knows on paper. Getting ready for lunch and moving between activities take him longer, which cuts into lesson time. He covers his ears during loud activities and leaves his seat to seek movement, so he misses parts of lessons. Occupational therapy would help him build the hand, self-care and sensory skills he needs to take part in the school day.  As a result he often finishes classwork late and joins fewer class activities than his classmates.

Services

Occupational therapy will be given by the school occupational therapist, or by a therapy assistant the therapist supervises. XX minutes of occupational therapy each week will take place outside the classroom and will work on hand skills, sensory processing and self-care.  Sessions may be one to one or in a small group.

Motor Goal
By March of 2028, with direct teaching of Fine Motor skills, XX  will reach 2 out of 3 objectives below in 80% of tries or on 3 out of 4 days when data is taken:
XX will improve fine motor cutting skills needed to manage classroom paper tasks by accurately cutting along a curved line within 1/4 inch of the boundary line.
XX will fasten the top button of his coat and engage the zipper pin, given a visual sequence card and no more than one verbal cue.
XX will improve visual motor skills needed to access written work by legibly copying letters and shapes with slanted lines (i.e. triangle, X, R, K, Q, Y, y).
Related Standards

1. HW.2.1. Prints letters and numbers that can be read on lined paper for the grade.
2. Tool use: M3.4 Uses crayons, pencils, scissors and modelling tools without help
3. Daily living skills, intermediate: Dresses and undresses, including buttons and fasteners
